what_it_does: When a large language model (an AI that generates text) is running and producing output word-by-word, it needs to keep a growing set of notes about everything it has seen so far — this running memory is often called a key-value cache. Managing where those notes live in physical memory is tricky: a popular technique called PagedAttention breaks the notes into small non-contiguous chunks to avoid waste, but that fragmented layout forces engineers to rewrite the math routines that read the notes and creates subtle slowdowns. vAttention takes a different approach: it reserves a large, contiguous block of virtual address space (the map the program uses to find memory) upfront, then relies on the operating system to fill in real physical memory only as each new chunk of notes is actually needed — a mechanism the OS already provides called demand paging. The result is that the math routines see a clean, unbroken address space and need no rewriting, while physical memory is still allocated frugally on demand, avoiding the fragmentation problem.
